Traced the Architecture diagram's directed edges (design.md:45-120). Two apparent cycles exist: (a) DETECT -> GEN (verdict) -> STAGE (candidate written) -> VALIDATE (pre-publish check) -> PUBLISHER (staged candidate PASSES) -> ANCHOR (publisher publishes anchor) -> DETECT (default-resolved trust anchor); (b) HANDSHAKE -> AGENT (challenge/nonce) -> GUARD (proposed tool call) -> AGENT (denial surfaced) -> HANDSHAKE (recorded result). Both were examined against design.md's own prose and found to be legitimate cross-invocation, temporal state-machine feedback loops (a later, separate invocation reads persisted state a prior, separate invocation wrote), not simultaneous structural/build/instantiation dependencies. The DETECT/ANCHOR loop is the design's deliberate trust-anchor mechanism, explicitly built to defeat a git-HEAD self-diffing attack (design.md 'Weakening-detector approved-context anchor CLI contract', lines 820-882, and 'New decision (closes B3)', lines 1357-1371: 'Git HEAD is trivially redefinable by an ordinary commit ... the anchor is instead the content a human actually last approved'). The HANDSHAKE/AGENT/GUARD loop is an explicit challenge/response security protocol (design.md 'New decision (defense-tier scope, B4)', lines 1287-1309). Neither loop creates an ambiguous build/initialization order or an implementation blocker. No structural (same-invocation, mutual) circular dependency was found.

design.md's `## ADR Change Log` (lines 268-281) states 'No new ADR. Every design decision this epic makes is already recorded in docs/adr/0016-workflow-axes-separation.md, 0018-provider-binding-separation.md, 0019-approval-sidecar-protection.md, 0020-conditional-predicate-dsl.md, and 0023-track-selection-contract-migration.md' -- and I verified all five files exist at those exact paths. However, design.md's own 'Human-copy publisher transactional bundle contract' (lines 911-1001) and its paired 'New decision (NEW -- multi-target atomicity)' Design Decision entry (lines 1382-1400) introduce a journaled, multi-target atomic-transaction protocol for the human-copy publisher: a prepare/journal/commit/complete sequence plus an automatic crash-recovery scan that converges every target to exactly one of two terminal states (all-pre or all-post), never a standing partial-publish mix (also restated in Security Boundaries B8, design.md:1481, and requirements.md Edge Cases, lines 2118-2127). This is a materially new integration pattern that is NOT covered by the ADR design.md itself cites as this mechanism's precedent: docs/adr/0011-phase2-handle-relative-protected-copy.md's own Consequences section states the opposite, explicitly-accepted limitation verbatim -- 'Each target rename is atomic, but the 18-target batch is not one transaction. A rename-time OS failure may leave a deterministic installed prefix and must be recovered with a reviewed full rollback batch' -- i.e. ADR-0011 explicitly accepts the exact partial-publish risk as an unautomated, human-reviewed residual, whereas design.md's new protocol claims automatic convergence to one of two terminal states with no human-reviewed rollback step. I additionally checked every other ADR in docs/adr/ (0001-0024, including 0021-context-projection-staleness.md and 0024-workflow-state-vs-project-context.md, neither of which addresses multi-file transaction/journaling semantics either) and found none that covers a journaled multi-target rename/crash-recovery protocol. Per this check's fallback rule: Feature introduces a journaled multi-target atomic-transaction protocol (Human-copy publisher transactional bundle contract, REQ-007) with no corresponding ADR -- the closest existing ADR (0011), which design.md itself cites as the pattern being 'generalized' (design.md:1529, 'generalizing ADR-0011'), explicitly disclaims the exact multi-target atomicity guarantee this design newly claims. design.md's own ADR Change Log closing text invites exactly this kind of impl-review judgment for a narrower case (OQ-001's approver-registry file, 'if impl-review disagrees, promoting it to its own ADR is a low-cost follow-up') but does not extend that same self-check to this transaction protocol.
